name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,366

entries.clue: Goal partly is to get to other side of pub (8)

blocks.note: to cross something is to get to the far side of it
a bar is the pub you drink in

annotation.surface: Part of the aim is simply getting to the far side of the pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Goal partly' asks for a piece of the goal rather than a synonym for it, which is fair but uncommon. The trap is reading 'Goal' as an ambition and hunting for a word meaning aim.
annotation.definitionFit: The crossbar is the horizontal bar joining the tops of the posts, so it is one component of a football goal rather than the whole frame.

entries.clue: Argument over a name for tree (5)

indicatorNotes.over: In a down entry a thing that is over another is written above it, so the argument sits on top of the letters that follow.

blocks.note: a row is a noisy argument
the clue's own article, taken as the single letter
n is the standard short form for name

annotation.surface: A quarrel about what to call a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: N for name is one of the alphabet's busiest abbreviations — north, new, noon and knight all queue behind it. 'Over' only confirms the order, since the clue already names its pieces in the order they are wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: The rowan is the mountain ash, a slim tree with red autumn berries found all over Britain, so 'tree' names it by kind.

entries.clue: Different, but not dry, warm weather (3)

indicatorNotes.but not: 'but not' excludes whatever it names, so those letters are struck out of the word standing before it.

blocks.note: sundry means various, a mixed set of different things
three letters to come out, spelt exactly as the clue writes them

annotation.surface: Weather that is unusual, not dry, and warm.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Different' makes it look like the first of three weather adjectives when it is in fact the whole of the raw material. Words meaning 'various' are worth collecting for exactly this kind of subtraction.
annotation.definitionFit: Sun is what people call the sunshine itself — 'we got a bit of sun' means bright warm weather, not the star.

entries.clue: Roman poet after black sheep, for one (5)

indicatorNotes.after: A thing that comes after another is written behind it, so the poet's letters follow the one standing for black.

blocks.note: b is the standard short form for black, as on a pencil
Ovid wrote the Metamorphoses in the reign of Augustus

annotation.surface: The family's black sheep, with a Roman poet trailing behind.
annotation.walkthrough: The idiom 'black sheep' is laid down to be read whole and then split down the middle: the colour is wordplay and the animal is the definition. Ovid is the Roman poet crosswords reach for first, with Virgil and Horace behind him.
annotation.definitionFit: The bovid family covers cattle, goats, antelope and sheep, so a sheep is one example of the group the answer names.

entries.clue: Short of oxygen, overtire poorly shipyard worker perhaps (7)

indicatorNotes.Short of: To be short of something is to be missing it, so the letter standing for oxygen is absent from the word that follows.
indicatorNotes.poorly: Something done poorly has not come out as it should, and letters in that state will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen, and it is the letter missing
the letters of 'overtire' with that O gone, seven for the pile

annotation.surface: Breathless and worn out, somebody is making a poor job of work in the docks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poorly' is British for unwell, so it reads as one more symptom beside 'short of oxygen' instead of as an instruction. Riveting is how ships' steel plates were fastened together before welding took the job over.
annotation.definitionFit: A riveter hammers home the rivets that hold steel plates together, one of the trades a shipyard is built on.

entries.clue: After break, this quick to make meal (4)

indicatorNotes.After: What stands after something begins where that thing ends, so only the tail of the longer word is wanted.

blocks.note: the meal the wanted letters complete once they are put in place
the five letters standing in front, which that meal's name opens with

annotation.surface: A quick meal thrown together once the break is over.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer's other meaning is the joke: to fast is to go without food, and breaking that fast is where the meal's name comes from. 'Quick' is the definition and has nothing to do with eating.
annotation.definitionFit: Fast is the everyday adjective for moving at speed, so it swaps straight in for quick.

entries.clue: Flippant aspect associated with debts (9)

blocks.note: one facet of a problem is one aspect of it
an IOU is a scribbled promise to pay, so debts are IOUs

annotation.surface: A light-hearted attitude to money owed.
annotation.walkthrough: IOU is 'I owe you' written down, and crosswords pluralise it freely. The answer is the stock example of a word carrying all five vowels once each and in alphabetical order.
annotation.definitionFit: To be facetious is to treat a serious matter with a joke, which is what flippant describes.

entries.clue: Put in chair I consumed stuff (7)

blocks.note: to sit a guest somewhere is to put them in a chair, and the past tense is wanted
the clue's own pronoun, taken as the single letter
what you consumed at dinner, you ate

annotation.surface: Sitting down, I ate whatever was going.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put in chair' is the transitive sit — you sit a visitor down — and the past tense is what the letters want. 'Stuff' is a verb here, the thing you do to a turkey, not a noun meaning things.
annotation.definitionFit: To satiate someone is to fill them right up with food, which is exactly what you do when you stuff them.

entries.clue: Small, pale bird (4)

blocks.note: S is the size on a clothing label
a wan face is pale and drained of colour

annotation.surface: A little bird with washed-out colouring.
annotation.walkthrough: S for small comes off a clothing label and turns up far more often than any bird. 'Wan' is the pallor of an ill face rather than of a faded paint.
annotation.definitionFit: A swan is the long-necked white waterbird of rivers and park lakes, so 'bird' names it by its family.

entries.clue: Vigour of big town, on examination (8)

indicatorNotes.on: In an across entry a thing placed on another has been written after it, so the town follows the examination.

blocks.note: a viva is the spoken examination a British degree ends with
a town grown big enough is a city

annotation.surface: A large town's liveliness being assessed.
annotation.walkthrough: A viva is short for viva voce, 'with the living voice', the oral exam a British student faces at the end of a degree. That Latin root is doing double duty, since the answer is built on the same 'living'.
annotation.definitionFit: Vivacity is liveliness of manner, the vigour of someone full of animation rather than physical strength.

entries.clue: Terrible to-do, then? Exactly (2,3,3)

indicatorNotes.Terrible: Something terrible is in a dreadful state, and letters in that state are not left standing in the order handed over.

blocks.note: eight letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling rather than their sense

annotation.surface: What a dreadful fuss that was, then — quite so.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Then?' looks like the hesitation of somebody fishing for agreement, which is how it slips into the pile of letters unnoticed. The phrase itself points at a clock face, where the dot is the exact mark a hand has to reach.
annotation.definitionFit: On the dot means at precisely the stated time, so 'exactly' is what you would say in its place.

entries.clue: Computer storage tough to control (4,5)

blocks.note: a tough problem is a hard one
to control a car is to drive it

annotation.surface: Computer storage that is difficult to manage.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface complaint splits exactly down the middle, each half a plain synonym, which is why nothing in it feels like wordplay at all. 'Drive' for control is the motoring sense rather than the urge.
annotation.definitionFit: A hard drive is the disk inside a machine that holds its files, which is what computer storage means.

entries.clue: Catch in mouth (4)

blocks.note: the verb: to take an animal or a person in a snare
the slang noun, as in an order to shut it

annotation.surface: Catching something in your mouth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Catch in mouth' reads as one phrase and is two definitions laid end to end, with nothing marking the seam between them. The mouth sense is slang and faintly rude; the catching sense is the plain verb.
annotation.definitionFit: To trap an animal is to catch it, and a trap is also the mouth in slang — 'shut your trap' is the usual outing.

entries.clue: Sign in the heavens divided us, I would say (6)

indicatorNotes.I would say: Saying it is the test: 'I would say' asks you to judge the words in front by the noise they make rather than by their spelling.

blocks.note: to divide a sheet of paper is to tear it, so the past tense of that comes before the clue's own 'us'

annotation.surface: Something in the sky came between us, I'd say.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Divided' has to be heard as 'tore' rather than 'split' or 'parted' — only that past tense makes the noise work. 'I would say' is the homophone marker, dressed up as somebody hedging an opinion.
annotation.definitionFit: Taurus is the bull, one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, and 'in the heavens' holds because it is a real constellation too.

entries.clue: A very quiet relaxation and calm (7)

blocks.note: the clue's own article, taken as the single letter
pp is pianissimo on a score, the direction to play very softly
a life of ease is one of relaxation

annotation.surface: A very quiet spell of relaxation and peace.
annotation.walkthrough: PP is pianissimo and P alone is piano, merely quiet, so the doubled letter is what 'very' buys. Musical dynamics are a standing supply of letters for setters.
annotation.definitionFit: To appease someone is to calm them by giving them what they are demanding, so it stands in for the verb calm.

entries.clue: Exceptional short period of work covering US agency (7)

indicatorNotes.short: Something cut short has lost its end, so the final letter of the word comes off.
indicatorNotes.covering: What covers a thing lies over it from both sides, so the letters in front close around the ones named next.

blocks.note: a spell is a stretch of time spent at a job, docked of its last letter
the Central Intelligence Agency, America's foreign intelligence service

annotation.surface: A brief stint of work spent shielding an American intelligence agency.
annotation.walkthrough: A spell is a stretch of time given over to something — 'a spell at the wheel' — and it is that sense, not the magic one, that gets docked. 'Covering' reads as protecting the agency while it is really wrapping round it.
annotation.definitionFit: Something special stands out from the ordinary run of things, which is what exceptional says of it.

entries.clue: We’re told ways to navigate island (6)

indicatorNotes.We’re told: Being told something is hearing it, so what follows is wanted as a noise rather than as a spelling.

blocks.note: roads are the ways you follow to get anywhere by land

annotation.surface: Directions for getting to an island, as reported to us.
annotation.walkthrough: Said aloud, the island and the everyday word for ways make the same noise; written down they share barely half their letters. 'We're told' is the marker — hearsay on the surface, sound underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: Rhodes is the largest of the Greek Dodecanese, a Mediterranean island substantial enough for 'island' alone to point at it.

entries.clue: Made haste with some furious pedalling (4)

indicatorNotes.some: 'some' asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it, and the part wanted is a run of consecutive letters.

blocks.note: four letters in a row here, straddling the gap between the two words

annotation.surface: Somebody got a move on with a burst of hard pedalling.
annotation.walkthrough: The letters wanted straddle a word boundary, which is where hidden answers are hardest to see: the eye reads a space as a full stop. 'Some' is the only word instructing anything; the rest is a cycling scene that happens to agree with the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To speed is to go fast, and its past tense is what you did if you made haste.

entries.clue: From trade fair, certain publicity (8)

blocks.note: an expo is a large trade exhibition
someone certain of a thing is sure of it

annotation.surface: A trade fair is bound to bring a measure of publicity.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Certain' reads as 'a certain amount of' and means 'sure', two senses sitting a long way apart. Expo is short for exposition, the old word for a great public show of goods.
annotation.definitionFit: Exposure is the publicity a person or product gets from being put in front of the public.

entries.clue: Add to one’s account years in agony (3,2)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts what stands before it inside what stands after, so the letter for years goes within the word for agony.

blocks.note: agony is pain at its sharpest
y is the short form for years, as on a form

annotation.surface: Years spent in torment.
annotation.walkthrough: Y for year or years comes off forms and timetables rather than dictionaries. The insertion word is doing the work while the surface wants it read as part of 'in agony'.
annotation.definitionFit: To pay in is to hand money across the counter so that it lands in your account, the bank's own phrase for topping up a balance.

entries.clue: Sudden attack nets pawn (5)

indicatorNotes.nets: A net closes round whatever it catches, so the word in front takes the letter named next inside it.

blocks.note: a raid is an attack made in and out again at speed
P is the pawn in chess notation

annotation.surface: A surprise raid takes a pawn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sudden attack' reads as one unit and is in fact a definition followed by its fodder, with the break falling in the middle of the phrase. Chess notation supplies the single letter, as it does for king, queen and knight.
annotation.definitionFit: Something rapid happens at great speed, and a change arriving that fast is felt as sudden.

entries.clue: Ivy, a tint used freely in Christmas scene (8)

indicatorNotes.used freely: To use something freely is to use it without restriction, and letters used that way need not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: eight letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling rather than their sense

annotation.surface: Ivy and a wash of colour applied generously to a Christmas display.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Used freely' sounds like advice to a decorator and is the shuffle. The fodder is disguised as more decoration, since ivy and a tint are just what you would expect in a sentence about Christmas.
annotation.definitionFit: The nativity is the stable tableau of the birth of Christ, the crib set out in churches and school halls every December.

entries.clue: Shy about page in text for printer (4)

indicatorNotes.about: What goes about a thing is wrapped round it, so the word in front takes the letter for page inside.

blocks.note: a coy answer is a shy one
p. is the standard short form of page in a reference

annotation.surface: Someone is bashful about a page of writing meant for the printer.
annotation.walkthrough: Copy is a newsroom word: a reporter files copy and a sub-editor cuts it, so 'good copy' means a good story. P for page comes off footnotes and indexes.
annotation.definitionFit: In publishing, copy is the written matter sent to be set in type — the words themselves rather than the finished page.

entries.clue: Mountain pass is chilly for the most part (3)

indicatorNotes.for the most part: Most of a word is all of it but the end, so the final letter drops away.

blocks.note: the plain four-letter word for chilly weather, before its end is docked

annotation.surface: A mountain pass is on the cold side.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For the most part' reads as a hedge on the statement and is an instruction to dock a letter. The word is French for neck, borrowed into English by mountaineers.
annotation.definitionFit: A col is the low saddle on a ridge between two peaks, which is exactly where a path crosses from one valley to the next.

entries.clue: Woman’s last to receive present (4)

indicatorNotes.last: 'last' asks for the final letter of the word it points at rather than the whole of it.

blocks.note: what belongs to a woman is hers, the possessive of she
the letter standing last in 'receive'

annotation.surface: The woman is the last one to be handed a gift.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Present' is the school-register sense — in the room, accounted for — and the parcels in the surface are there to stop you seeing it. 'Last to receive' sounds like a place in a queue and points at a final letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Answering 'here' at a roll call is how you say you are present, so the two words swap in and out of that sentence.

entries.clue: Letter from countrywoman following separation (8)

indicatorNotes.following separation: A thing that follows separation has been pulled apart, so the compound word in front is read as its two halves and each half swapped for a synonym.

blocks.note: split in two, the compound opens with 'country', and a country is a land
the same compound's second half is 'woman', and a lady is a woman

annotation.surface: A letter arrives from a woman in the country after a break-up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Separation' is a marriage coming apart on the surface and a compound word coming apart underneath. 'Letter' is one who lets, said as let-er, and the alphabet has nothing to do with it.
annotation.definitionFit: A landlady lets out rooms or a flat, and one who lets is a letter — the trade noun, not the thing that comes in the post.
